summary: Defines a DHCP option that lets a server give a client a list of static routes. Unlike older options, each route's destination is classless and includes a subnet mask, so modern address layouts can be described.

plainLanguage.summary: When a computer joins a network, the server can hand it a list of side roads and where they lead. This option lets that list use flexible-size neighborhoods.

questions: how does dhcp classless static route encoding work
what is the dhcp router option 0.0.0.0 route
subtitle: How a DHCP server can hand a client a list of routes whose destinations carry their own subnet masks.

tldr.problem: The DHCP options from RFC 2132 can only install a default route or a table of classful routes, where the subnet mask is implied by the network number. Classless routing is what is mostly deployed, so that table is no longer useful.
tldr.mechanism: A new DHCP option, code 121, carries one or more static routes. Each route is a compact destination descriptor (mask width plus only the significant octets of the subnet number) followed by a 4-byte router address.
tldr.outcome: A client that supports the option installs these routes and ignores the Router option and the older Static Routes option (option 33), which this option obsoletes.

today: RFC 3442 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2132, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself states that the option obsoletes the Static Routes option (option 33).

sections.title: Why Classful Static Routes Fall Short
sections.content:
An IP host uses routers to reach hosts on other subnets. Using DHCP to fill its routing table has several virtues: it reuses messages that would be sent anyway, it needs little extra work because the DHCP server is already maintained, and it needs no additional infrastructure.

The DHCP protocol in RFC 2131 and the options in RFC 2132 only offer a default route or a table of classful routes, where the subnet mask is implicit in the subnet number. The RFC says classful routing is no longer in common use, so the Static Routes option (option 33) is no longer useful. In classless routing a host must know both the network number and the subnet mask.

The new option provides a subnet mask for each entry, so the mask can be something other than what the classful algorithm would give. The RFC states that this option obsoletes option 33.
sections.plainLanguage: The old list only worked if every neighborhood was one of a few fixed sizes. The new list lets each neighborhood be any size, because it says the size out loud.

sections.title: The Classless Route Option Format
sections.content:
The option code is 121 and its minimum length is 5 bytes. It holds one or more static routes. Each route is a destination descriptor followed by the 4-byte IP address of the router to use for that destination.

A destination descriptor is one octet giving the width of the subnet mask, followed by only the significant octets of the subnet number. The width is the number of one bits in the mask, so 10.0.127.0 with mask 255.255.255.0 has width 24. The significant octets are those where the mask octet is non-zero, which is the width divided by eight, rounded up.

For example, 10.0.0.0 with 255.0.0.0 is written 8.10, and 10.229.0.128 with 255.255.255.128 is written 25.10.229.0.128. A default route (subnet 0, mask 0) is just 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing the whole address and the whole mask, each entry says how many leading numbers matter and then lists just those. It is like writing only the first few digits of a phone number when the area is already clear.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
A client that does not support the option MUST ignore it. A client that supports it MUST install the routes, and MUST NOT install routes from the Static Routes option (option 33) if both are provided. If the server sends both a Classless Static Routes option and a Router option, the client MUST ignore the Router option.

A supporting client that sends a Parameter Request List MUST request both this option and the Router option. It MAY also request the Static Routes option for older servers, but the Classless Static Routes code MUST appear before the Router and Static Routes codes in the list.

After decoding each descriptor, the client MUST zero any bits of the subnet number where the mask bit is zero. For example, a route to 129.210.177.132 with mask 255.255.255.128 is installed as 129.210.177.128.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer that understands the new list uses it and puts the old lists aside. It also tidies each entry so only the neighborhood part of the address is kept.

sections.title: Local Subnet Routes
sections.content:
Sometimes more than one IP subnet is configured on the same link, so a host in one subnet could talk directly to a host in another. For each other subnet on the link, the server MAY specify a router address of 0.0.0.0.

The RFC gives an example with three subnets on a link: 10.0.0/24, 192.168.0/24 and 10.0.21/24. A client assigned 10.0.21.17 could get a route to 10.0.0/24 and one to 192.168.0/24, each with router address 0.0.0.0.

A client whose TCP/IP stack does not support this MUST ignore routes whose router address is 0.0.0.0. This behavior applies only to the Classless Static Routes option, not to the Static Routes or Router options.
sections.plainLanguage: If several neighborhoods share the same street, the server can say there is no door to go through: just walk straight there. A computer that cannot do that skips those entries.

sections.title: Message Size and Server Configuration
sections.content:
A full routing table can be large, and the standard 576 octet maximum DHCP message size may be too short. Clients SHOULD therefore send a Maximum DHCP Message Size option if their stack can receive larger datagrams, with a value of at least the MTU of the interface being configured. Clients and servers MUST also implement DHCP option concatenation from RFC 3396, because this is a concatenation-requiring option.

Many clients may not implement the option, so administrators should configure servers to send both a Router option and a Classless Static Routes option, listing the default routers in both. However, when a client requests the classless option and the server is sending it, the server SHOULD NOT include the Router or Static Routes options.
sections.plainLanguage: A long list may not fit in a small envelope, so the computer asks for a bigger one. The server also keeps the old-style note around for computers that cannot read the new one.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The option can misdirect traffic by supplying incorrect router addresses. That can be a denial of service, if the router address is simply invalid, or a man-in-the-middle attack, if it is the address of a potential snooper. The RFC notes this is not a new problem, since the Router and Static Routes options in RFC 2132 have the same vulnerability. It points to section 7 of RFC 2131 and to RFC 3118 for DHCP security.

IANA allocated option code 121 for this option.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone gives a computer a bad map, it can end up sending its mail to the wrong place, even to a snoop. The old maps had the same weakness.
